name: WikiTableQuestions
summary: 4,344 questions about single Wikipedia tables, each answered by reading, comparing, counting, or computing over the cells of a table the question's writer had in front of them.
overview:
WikiTableQuestions asks questions about a table. Each task shows one table taken from a Wikipedia page and a question a person wrote about it, and the answer is whatever the table says, which is often not written in any single cell: the answer may require comparing rows, counting them, taking a maximum, adding values, or reading a cell and then looking something up elsewhere in the table. The dataset was introduced by Panupong Pasupat and Percy Liang at ACL 2015 as a test for semantic parsing over semi-structured data, and it remains the standard benchmark for question answering over tables. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1508.00305)

The authors sampled data tables at random from Wikipedia, keeping those with at least 8 rows and 5 columns, and collected questions on Amazon Mechanical Turk in two passes. In the first, workers wrote trivia questions about a table they were shown, each prompted by one of 36 generic instructions such as asking that the question require a calculation, which pushed them past simple lookups. In the second, other workers answered those questions from the same table, and a question was kept only when at least two workers agreed on the answer; about 69% survived. The result is 22,033 questions over 2,108 tables. A later dataset, Squall, added hand-written SQL equivalents for 17,553 of those examples, which the project page links. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1508.00305) and [project page](https://ppasupat.github.io/WikiTableQuestions/)

The difficulty is that a model must work out the operation as well as the answer. The authors' semantic parser, which searched candidate logical forms over the table, reached 37.1% accuracy on the test set, against 12.7% for an information retrieval baseline, while the correct answer appeared somewhere among its candidate logical forms for 76.6% of questions. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1508.00305)
methodology:
This snapshot contains the complete official test split, `data/pristine-unseen-tables.tsv`, at the pinned commit: 4,344 questions over 421 tables, chosen so that none of its tables appear in the training data. The training split of 14,152 questions, the 3,537 questions over tables already seen in training, the five random development splits of the training data, and the 300 questions annotated with gold logical forms are not imported. The data files have not changed since version 1.0.2 was imported into the repository in February 2017; the pinned commit is the current head and only touches documentation after that. [Test split at the pinned commit](https://github.com/ppasupat/WikiTableQuestions/blob/7d455a5a707b96341ef72aff9428749d443d8aa9/data/pristine-unseen-tables.tsv)

Each Task Prompt is the question, a line naming the Wikipedia page the table was extracted from, and the table itself as the upstream comma-separated file, reproduced verbatim inside a fenced block. Inlining the table keeps each task self-contained, which is why this snapshot repeats a table once per question asked about it; the Environment link on each task points at the single upstream table file. The tables in this split run from 6 to 518 rows including their header, and from 3 to 21 columns, averaging 28 rows and 6 columns; the paper describes sampling tables with at least 8 rows and 5 columns, but 39 of these tables have fewer than 8 data rows and 40 have fewer than 5 columns. Benchopedia reproduces the comma-separated form; the upstream snapshot also carries each table as a tab-separated file, as a column-aligned text file the authors warn is lossy, as the extracted HTML table, and as the raw HTML of the whole page, none of which are imported. [Table files at the pinned commit](https://github.com/ppasupat/WikiTableQuestions/tree/7d455a5a707b96341ef72aff9428749d443d8aa9/csv)

The Solution is the reference answer. 4,229 of the questions have a single answer and 115 have a list, which upstream stores pipe-separated and this snapshot writes one item per line; the longest has 27 items. Answers are the strings the Mechanical Turk workers agreed on, so they usually appear verbatim in the table but may be a count or a computed number that does not. IDs are the upstream example IDs, nu-0 through nu-4343. The CoreNLP-tagged copies of the questions and tables, which carry the tokenisation and the canonical number and date values the official evaluator reads, are not imported.

Every table's Wikipedia provenance is recorded. The upstream metadata beside each table names the page and the exact revision the table was taken from, the page title appears in the prompt, and the importer regenerates ATTRIBUTION.md with all 421 pages and permalinks to those revisions. Five of the 421 pages have since been deleted from Wikipedia and 82 others have been renamed, which the redistribution review records. The importer uses only Python's standard library and can be rerun with python3 data/wikitablequestions/import.py.
scoring:
A model answers with a value or a list of values, and the official evaluator decides whether that denotation matches the reference. The lists must be the same size, and every reference item must match some predicted item. Two items match if their normalised strings are identical, where normalising removes diacritics, converts smart quotes and dashes to ASCII, strips trailing citation markers and bracketed or parenthesised trailing details, removes surrounding quotation marks and a trailing period, lowercases, and collapses whitespace. An item also matches if the reference can be read as a number and the prediction is the same number, or as a date and the prediction is the same date with every field equal. The score is the share of questions answered correctly; there is no partial credit for a partly right list. [Official evaluator](https://github.com/ppasupat/WikiTableQuestions/blob/7d455a5a707b96341ef72aff9428749d443d8aa9/evaluator.py)

The evaluator expects the tagged copy of the split, because it uses the CoreNLP values stored there to decide whether a reference string is a number or a date. The authors note that scores from the official evaluator differ from those their SEMPRE codebase reports, since SEMPRE additionally requires the prediction to have the same type as the reference, and that the official evaluator is the more lenient of the two. The published script is Python 2 code. [Repository README](https://github.com/ppasupat/WikiTableQuestions/blob/7d455a5a707b96341ef72aff9428749d443d8aa9/README.md#evaluator)

Results are reported on this test split, with development results coming from the random splits of the training data; a number computed on the seen-tables portion or on one of those development splits is not comparable with a test score. Benchopedia stores the questions, tables, and reference answers. It does not run the evaluator or publish model scores for this snapshot.
limitations:
The answers were agreed by two crowdworkers, not adjudicated by experts, and scoring compares strings after normalisation, so what counts as right depends on how the reference was phrased. A model that answers a question about a person with the full name, where the worker wrote the surname, is marked wrong; a correct list with one extra or missing item is wrong outright. The normalisation rules were tuned on this data and strip parenthesised detail and trailing citations, which helps with Wikipedia's footnote markers but also hides real differences. [Official evaluator](https://github.com/ppasupat/WikiTableQuestions/blob/7d455a5a707b96341ef72aff9428749d443d8aa9/evaluator.py)

The questions were written by people looking at one table, with instructions to make them require calculation, so they are deliberately unlike questions a person would ask without the table in front of them, and the operations they need reflect the 36 prompts the authors used. Every question is answerable from its own table, so nothing here tests searching for a table, combining several, noticing that the table does not contain the answer, or reading a table rendered as anything other than text. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1508.00305)

The tables are converted HTML from Wikipedia pages as they stood around 2015, and the conversion flattened their structure: merged cells, footnotes, and images were turned into plain cell text, and the authors warn that their own column-aligned rendering lost information. Five of the 421 source pages have since been deleted from Wikipedia and 82 have been renamed, so a reader who checks the data against the live encyclopedia will not always find the same table. A question about what a table says is answered by this snapshot of it, not by the current article.

The data is public, has no canary string, and has been studied for a decade, so a model may have seen these tables, questions, and answers in training. The split is also narrow in another way: all 4,344 questions come from 421 tables, so a model that happens to handle a few large or unusual tables well can move the score more than the question count suggests.
